title: These Mobile Apps Can Keep You Connected - MOAA
description:
ReleVote (Apple | Android): Like the app above, ReleVote touts its ability to track activity across all three branches of the federal government.
Defense & Military News (Apple | Android): Find military and defense news in one spot, including videos, tech updates, and reviews.
Health Care VA: Health and Benefits (Apple | Android): This official VA app helps veterans manage health care, benefits, and payments.
(Fee-based) Babies on the Homefront (Android): Military parents can stay connected with family by sharing experiences through this app while a servicemember is on deployment.
Hero Care (Apple | Android): This American Red Cross app helps families navigate the challenges of service and deployment.
text:
(This article by Charlsy Panzino originally appeared in the November 2026 issue of Military Officer magazine.)

As a member of the uniformed services community, you have a lot to keep track of. Why not make things a little simpler with software?

From news to health care to life at installations and more, we’ve rounded up some of the most useful apps out there, with many available through both the Google and Apple app stores.

All of these are free unless otherwise stated.

News and Legislation

Congress Vote Tracker (Apple): This app makes it easier to keep up with military-related legislation by letting users follow bills and congressional activity. Users can also see voting records for members of Congress.

ReleVote (Apple | Android): Like the app above, ReleVote touts its ability to track activity across all three branches of the federal government.

Defense & Military News (Apple | Android): Find military and defense news in one spot, including videos, tech updates, and reviews. This app compiles news stories from several prominent outlets.

Stars & Stripes (Apple | Android): Like its website, this app provides updates on breaking news, military life, benefits, and pay, plus the latest on global conflicts, deployments, and Pentagon policy — all in the palm of your hand.

[HAVE A NEWS READER APP? Add MOAA’s Newsfeed]

Finance

YNAB (You Need a Budget) (Apple | Android): YNAB uses a method of “giving every dollar a job,” where each dollar is assigned to an expense category based on what’s important and when it’s due. The user checks their plan before spending and can make changes by moving money between categories. (Cost: 34-day free trial, then $14.99 per month.)

Military Money: Pay & Pension (Apple): Calculate service pay, including current Basic Allowance for Housing, Basic Allowance for Subsistence, and special duty pay, along with budgeting and planning for retirement.

US Military Pay Calculator (Apple | Android): This is similar to the app above. As always, consult a professional for the most accurate information.

[RELATED: Financial Calculators From MOAA]

Commissary Click2Go (Apple | Android): Users can order same-day groceries from their commissary at the same in-store prices, with access to sales and special offers to help military families save money.

Health Care

VA: Health and Benefits (Apple | Android): This official VA app helps veterans manage health care, benefits, and payments. Users can refill and track prescriptions, message their health care team, and review appointments. They can also check their disability rating, review claims or appeal statuses, and submit evidence for claims or appeals.

TRICARE East (Apple | Android): TRICARE users in the East Region can use the newly rebranded app to make payments, check eligibility, and find a provider. The app also allows users to view, print, share, and email their explanation of benefits and referral letters. As of this writing, there is no app for the West Region. However, those in the area can use Tri- West Healthcare Alliance’s mobile portal.

[RELATED: More Health Care News From MOAA]

VA Video Connect (Apple | Android): This secure videoconferencing app lets veterans and their caregivers meet with VA health care providers via telehealth, which is especially useful for those with limited access to VA facilities or who can’t regularly attend in-person appointments.

Non-Health Benefits

VetsApp (Apple | Android): Created by veterans, for veterans, VetsApp offers a central point for military discounts and deals, quick access to VA benefits, payment calculators, and curated lists of free events and virtual job fairs.

MyVetBENEFITS (Apple | Android): This app matches users with benefits they’re most likely eligible for. This is useful whether you’re a new recruit exploring benefits for the first time, a servicemember transitioning to civilian life, or a veteran, caregiver, or surviving family member. MyVetBENEFITS offers a personalized benefits list and direct access to employment, health and wellness, and financial services.

Professional Development

LinkedIn (Apple | Android): Although not specific to the uniformed services community, LinkedIn is still one of the best places to network and find jobs. Building a strong network on the platform helps users share opportunities, offer referrals, and provide mentorship. A strong profile also increases visibility for recruiters looking for transitioning servicemembers and veterans. LinkedIn Learning offers online classes to build new skills, free for the military community through ACT Now Education.

[RELATED: MOAA on Linkedin]

MilEd Benefits (Apple | Android): Servicemembers can use the MilEd Benefits app to find free education benefits that support military advancement or completing a college degree, along with resources for those transitioning to civilian jobs.

Military Moving

Sortly (Apple | Android): Users can track, organize, and manage their assets while moving, which can be a huge help when starting a PCS journey. Users can sort items by room or box and upload photos to easily identify their possessions. (Includes pay tiers.)

Vet Tix (Apple | Android): Find something to do around your new home — for free. Veteran Tickets Foundation’s Tickets for Troops Program works with major sports teams, leagues, promoters, organizations, venues, and more to provide free tickets to servicemembers and veterans.

The Big Moving Adventure (Apple | Android): This Sesame Street app lets kids create a Muppet friend who helps them through the moving process, whether they recently moved or have one coming up. The app guides families through packing, expressing feelings, making new friends, and exploring their new home.

Military Family

Sandboxx (Apple | Android): Families can send letters to recruits in basic training through Sandboxx, which also provides installation-specific training updates and news. Users write digital letters that are printed and mailed overnight to any recruiting base, and families can add gift cards to their letters. (Fee-based)

Babies on the Homefront (Android): Military parents can stay connected with family by sharing experiences through this app while a servicemember is on deployment. The app offers tips for handling tough parenting moments, ideas for playtime (even when away from home), and a way to upload information on the child’s development and life milestones.

Hero Care (Apple | Android): This American Red Cross app helps families navigate the challenges of service and deployment. Hero Care provides emergency communication between servicemembers and families through a free, confidential, 24/7 network. The app also explains Red Cross services offered before, during, and after deployment, along with information about VA facilities, benefits, job resources, and mental health programs.

Life at Installations

My Army Post (Apple | Android): This app, which replaced Digital Garrison, provides centralized information for specific posts. Get real-time alerts about gate traffic and closures; hours of operation for restaurants, gyms, hospitals, and commissaries; and information for base events, activities, and announcements.

MCCS Connect (Apple | Android): Marine Corps Community Services created this app to help Marines and sailors and their families find installation-specific information in one place. The app provides information on services, events, and activities.

App Locker: Access more than 80 Navy-approved apps in one spot, including information for specific bases and naval stations.

GuideOn Military (Apple | Android): The Air Force discontinued its USAF Connect app in favor of providing base updates on social media and base-specific websites, but airmen can use the GuideOn Military app to help fill the gaps. Created by a military spouse, users can search for directions, units, events, and more at different installations.

USSF Guardian One (Apple | Android): Guardians can use this app to find base information along with Space Force-specific news, resources, and updates from senior leaders. The app also includes publicly visible content to support family members.

USCG Work-Life (Apple | Android): Coast Guardsmen and their families can access information on work-life programs, housing, and activities, and get real-time updates on current events.

NOAA Directory (Apple): NOAA officers are mission-based without dedicated installations, but they can use the agency’s staff directory app to search for personnel. They can also use service-specific apps depending on where they’re assigned.

TotalForce+

MOAA’s annual TotalForce+ conference — the first and only military conference where people outrank everything — returns Feb. 1-3, 2027, at the Gaylord National Resort & Convention Center in National Harbor, Md. If you’re planning on attending, be sure to download the TotalForce+ app in the weeks leading up to the conference. The app will be available in Apple’s App Store and on Google Play.

Charlsy Panzino is a writer based in Boise, Idaho.

text:
(This article by Hope Hodge Seck originally appeared in the November 2026 issue of Military Officer magazine.)

Addressing a crowd of U.S. military generals and flag officers in Quantico, Va., in September 2025, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth deplored the “tiring” sight of “fat troops” in formation and “fat generals and admirals in the halls of the Pentagon.” He wanted change — and it had to begin right away.

By the time the 45-minute speech was over, new directives were landing in the inboxes of military commanders around the globe, laying out strict new requirements for military fitness, including twice-annual fitness assessments; a common way of measuring body composition; and a gender-neutral, but age-graded, physical qualification test for all troops in combat specialties.

“The new War Department Golden Rule is this: Do unto your unit as you would have done unto your own child’s unit,” Hegseth said. “Would you want him serving with fat or unfit or under-trained troops or alongside people who can’t meet basic standards or in a unit where standards were lowered so certain types of troops could make it in, in a unit where leaders were promoted for reasons other than merit, performance, and war fighting? The answer is not just no; it’s hell no.”

A Fitness Reset

The problem is well-established. A December 2025 military health system study shows the proportion of overweight and obese active duty troops dramatically increased from 2013 to 2023, with mid-2019 representing an “inflection point.” Obesity among male troops increased from 18.1% in 2019 to 25.3% in 2023, and among female troops from 12% to 19.6%. The study’s authors noted the steep increase was likely explained by the COVID-19 pandemic, which prompted the services, to varying extents, to suspend physical fitness testing.

Marines participate in the obstacle course at Marine Corps Air Station Beaufort, S.C., on April 6. (Photo by Cpl. Isabella Renaud/Marine Corps)

Hegseth’s fitness mandate sent service leaders in a race to prepare their troops for the change and roll out new guidance. For some services, the unambiguous message from the top was a clarifying kick start for long-discussed new fitness initiatives; for others, it competes with more holistic paths they’ve charted toward a common goal of advancing total force readiness. Experts who spoke to Military Officer recognized the need for a fitness overhaul but cautioned that abrupt implementation might lead to unintended consequences like injuries or sidelining fit troops who don’t match a strict mold.

In the Air Force, the implementation of a new scored physical training (PT) test on July 1 — after a six-month unscored diagnostic period that began in March — was met by some with despair. Among the changes were a 2-mile run that replaced the previous 1.5-mile run, and score charts that, in many cases, required troops to do more repetitions on exercises like pushups and situps to earn the same points they had before.

An anonymous poster on the online forum Reddit complained the Air Force standards were “out of touch” and more appropriate for special operators.

“Most of us work 12 hour shifts on the flightline or sit behind a desk coding all day, when are we suppose to train for a 2 mile run?” the user wrote.

Candidates in Special Warfare Assessment and Selection perform pullups wearing 20 pound weight vests before sprinting to the next activity during the Pararescue Memorial workout on Joint Base San Antonio-Lackland, Texas, on April 7. (Photo by Jennifer Gangemi/Air Force)

But according to Air Force officials, the diagnostic period proved airmen, by and large, could get it done. In that period, according to Col. Marjorie Barnum, the chief of the Air Force’s Military Force Policy Division at the Manpower, Personnel, and Services Directorate, 40,000 tests were recorded, and the standard proved an “adequate assessment” of fitness across gender and age demographics.

“We do think we may have missed some demographics in that initial testing window, and so we’ll continue to receive and analyze data,” Barnum said, adding that fewer airmen over the age of 50 were represented in the data and that those most at risk of failing the test were less likely to have taken it during the nondiagnostic period, leaving the fittest troops overrepresented. She also said the Air Force planned to clarify guidance about a directive to get physical training done every duty day, as that move had caused some consternation within the force.

While the full impact of the stricter fitness test remains unclear, Hegseth’s directive did prove the catalyst for launching another initiative for the Air Force: a Master Fitness Leader (MFL) program that kicked off its first training course in March and had, as of July, graduated 325 leaders distributed throughout the force.

[FROM AF.MIL: MFL Course Enhances New USAF Fitness Mindset]

The idea to develop airmen who could guide their peers in safe and effective physical training had long been “discussed and in the works,” said Chief Master Sgt. Bobby Drayton, a career field manager. “Once the shift came down and the messaging came down from [the secretary of war], it definitely prompted us to roll out a little faster and make it a top priority,” he said.

A Marine with 2nd Marine Aircraft Wing participates in physical training at Marine Corps Air Station Cherry Point, N.C., on Aug. 17. (Photo by Cpl. Mya Seymour/Marine Corps)

Beyond the PT Test

Hegseth’s line in the sand had the same effect for the Navy’s Human Performance Optimization (HPO) Program, which rolled out as a San Diego-based pilot in February after 12 years of internal development. The program, similar to the Army’s well-received Holistic Health and Fitness (H2F) Program, aims to aid in injury prevention, sleep, nutrition, and cognitive enhancement in addition to increasing fitness test scores.

[RELATED: Navy HPO | Army H2F]

“I think with the new leadership and the new direction and the new desire to support the human hardware, it was perfectly aligned and perfectly timed to jump on this human performance optimization effort and run with it,” said Tunde Ridley, fitness branch director for Navy Installations Command.

With 17 commands now involved and plans to take the program aboard ships, leaders say they’re seeing great success from the pilot. In one case, according to Capt. Brian Bungay, commander of Naval Base San Diego, leaders were approached by the commander of USS Higbee (DDG-123) with a pressing need: 20 sailors who failed their last fitness assessment needed to get back to regulations.

Through the HPO Program, the sailors were fed into a remediation initiative involving workouts up to four times per week and, Bungay said, were ultimately able to pass the test.

Bungay noted the program helped him increase his own physical fitness assessment score year over year and allowed him to max out his plank hold.

A sailor assigned to the Pre-Commissioning Unit John F. Kennedy (CVN-79) lifts weights as part of a 1,000-pound fitness challenge during acceptance trials on Aug. 14. (Photo by Mass Communication Specialist 1st Class Sean Gallagher/Navy)

A Common Standard

Not all the services had the same distance to travel when implementing Hegseth’s mandate for a gender-neutral combat-qualifying test. The Navy, which had never had a combat-specific test, assembled experts from the special operations and explosive ordnance disposal communities to develop an “initial look at what a [combat fitness test] can be,” said Lt. Cmdr. Maile Richert, a professor in the Department of Military and Emergency Medicine at Uniformed Services University.

The test involves an 800-meter swim with fins, plus pushups, pullups, and a timed run, all while wearing a 20-pound weighted vest. The test, which began as a requirement July 1 and applies to just four job specialties, is likely to be much more difficult than the Army’s new combat field test, which will be administered for 24 jobs.

The Army’s version of the test — based, per Hegseth’s direction, on the service’s existing Expert Physical Fitness Assessment — includes a seven-event exercise sequence involving movement and carry drills, bookended by 1-mile runs.

“We took this as an opportunity to look at ourselves and examine inwardly how we were evaluating fitness and how we were promulgating physical readiness for soldiers,” said Maj. Alex Boroff, then a Training Management Directorate action officer for the Army.

The new test follows the Army’s blighted efforts to roll out a gender- and age-neutral Army Combat Fitness Test for all soldiers that included an upper-body isolation event and the leg tuck. The move had prompted immediate outcry, with critics saying it was hard to train for and caused disproportionate failure rates among women. After a decade of development, the test would be Army policy for just three years, getting replaced by the gender- and age-specific Army Fitness Test in 2025.

American soldiers and allied forces take part in the Day of Bir Hakeim 10K mud race at Tapa Army Base, Estonia, on June 10. (Photo by Staff Sgt. Olivia Lauer/Army)

The Army rolled out the Combat Field Test in April 2026, steering clear of leg tucks and cautiously giving soldiers a yearlong diagnostic period to take the test without consequences so the service can adjust it if the data reveals a concern.

While test results are still filtering in, the Army in July dropped another big update for soldiers: a new waist-to-height ratio body composition evaluation, to be undergone twice a year, per Hegseth’s direction. There’s little recourse for soldiers who don’t fall within the prescribed ratio of less than 0.55; the Army’s new policy does away with previous exemptions for exceptionally fit and muscular soldiers or secondary testing methods, like the DEXA scan bone density test, for troops who want to contest the tape test’s accuracy.

This is despite a 2023 study by the U.S. Army Research Institute of Environmental Medicine of nearly 2,700 soldiers that had formed the basis for the Army’s previous body composition system and guided the service in crafting backup options.

Alex Morrow, a host of the tactical human performance podcast MOPs & MOEs and an Army reservist, said he wondered if the service’s choice to build a strict no-exceptions policy was intended to provoke a crisis that might force the Pentagon to take notice.

“The populations that’ll get weird are shorter men and then specifically postpartum women,” Morrow said. “And I think when the service starts to see some examples of very fit people from those categories failing and having no recourse, it’ll be easy to tell those stories.”

For its part, the Marine Corps kept the high-performance tape test exemption and the backup screening option, using a technology known as bioelectrical impedance. But the Corps also adapted a stricter waist-to-height ratio requirement than the Army: 0.52.

Benjamin McAndrews, head of the service’s human performance branch, said the Corps chose that standard because it represented “early risk detection,” adding that the impact of the more exacting standard on the force will take time to become clear.

A sailor sprints up a ramp during a physical training event in the hanger bay of USS Boxer (LHD-4) on June 16. (Photo by Sgt. Trent A. Henry/Marine Corps)

The Readiness Paradox

To varying extents, the services are waiting for data to show the impact of the changes rolling out to the force. While additional Pentagon memos released in May stress the value of “Warfighter Performance Optimization” and promise upcoming programming to bring together best practices in regard to holistic health, leverage wearable technology, and shore up brain health, a former head of human performance for the Marine Corps worries the initial jolt toward higher fitness standards and accountability will take its toll as injuries.

“Daily training without programming, periodization, and recovery isn’t fitness — it’s an injury pipeline,” said Col. Brian McGuire, USMCR (Ret), who now runs his own human performance advisory firm. “Musculoskeletal injury is already the single-largest driver of lost duty days and medical non-deployability in the force. A directive that increases training volume without resourcing the human performance infrastructure to manage it can, paradoxically, reduce the readiness it’s trying to build.”

Still, Morrow and McGuire see value and opportunity for the services to prioritize fitness and hold troops to a higher, data-driven standard, particularly after years of post-COVID-19 backsliding.

“For some branches, it absolutely has been the kick in the pants they needed,” Morrow said, adding that he had observed a “culture change” brought on by the return to daily PT sessions.

But for services that invested in specialized ways to achieve common fitness goals, it’s uncertain how much flexibility there will be to divert from Pentagon mandates in pursuing those paths.

Guardians stretch before beginning the Delta 12 Summer Fitness Challenge Physical Training Field Day at Peterson Space Force Base, Colo., on Sept. 12, 2025. (Photo by Keefer Patterson/Space Force)

A Different Measure

The Space Force, the youngest and smallest of all the branches under the Pentagon, has championed “continuous fitness assessments” over semiannual ones, using Garmin Instinct watches to hold troops accountable to complete “regular, purposeful physical activity,” said Christine Heit, the service’s head of holistic health assessments. While the Space Force did roll out a human performance evaluation that complies with Pentagon mandates, leaders continue to work on turning the wearables-based assessment into a program of record by next year.

“You can perform great and do great on your physical fitness assessment, or you might not be feeling well that day, or the temperature might be a little hot, and you don’t perform as well as you could,” Heit said of the traditional test. “The study totally eliminates that because it’s based on heart rate, and heart rate doesn’t change over time, so we’re actually able to measure health and cardiorespiratory fitness instead of one’s ability to perform during a test on a specific day.”

Once the service has a validated program, it could ask the Pentagon for an exemption from conventional testing. But leaders aren’t yet ready to commit to an action plan.

“We’re still likely going to be the first service to develop an enterprise-wide wearable program,” Heit said. “How that’s going to impact our way forward for physical fitness, I can’t share yet because I just don’t know. We’re going to see what we can accomplish.”

Recruits exercise at Coast Guard Training Center Cape May, N.J., on March 30. (Photo by Petty Officer 3rd Class Danielle Layton/Coast Guard)

Coast Guard Makes History

For the first time since its establishment in 1790, the U.S. Coast Guard debuted a mandatory physical fitness test for all members on July 1, citing, among other things, increased attention and resources flowing to the service amid high operational tempo. While the Coast Guard ranks somewhere in the middle among the services for obesity, a 2021 data analysis from the think tank Rand found nearly 67% of its personnel were overweight or obese.

Rear Adm. Christopher Hulser, who spoke in his previous role as chief of staff and executive assistant to the commandant of the Coast Guard, said the service’s fitness culture has been siloed, with high motivation among elite fields like rescue swimmers and little incentive for workouts in other jobs.

Uniquely among the services, the Coast Guard opted to make the test binding for officers and senior leaders first, a move intended to show that accountability flowed from the top down. The service also handed leaders the responsibility of ensuring their subordinates had time to conduct daily exercise during the workday.

“What [Coast Guard Commandant Adm. Kevin Lunday] wanted to … show the fleet ... is we take care of ourselves; we take care of physical readiness as part of our duty,” Hulser said.

The new fitness test, which may be revised as performance data comes in, includes pushups, a timed forearm plank, and a choice of cardio events, including running, rowing, or swimming.

Hope Hodge Seck is a writer in Massachusetts.

text:
(This article originally appeared in the November 2026 issue of Military Officer magazine.)

The Pentagon has extended a TRICARE Childbirth and Breastfeeding Support Demonstration (CBSD) that covers support services from certified nonmedical labor doulas, certified lactation consultants, and certified lactation counselors for certain TRICARE beneficiaries.

The demonstration, which was authorized as part of the FY 2021 National Defense Authorization Act, originally ran from January 2022 through December 2026 but now runs through the end of 2031.

The CBSD is available to beneficiaries enrolled in TRICARE Prime, TRICARE Prime Remote, and TRICARE Select; plus, as of January 2025, the expansion provides coverage for those overseas. It is unavailable for beneficiaries enrolled in TRICARE For Life, the US Family Health Plan, or the Continued Health Care Benefit Program.

[FROM TRICARE.MIL: TRICARE Childbirth and Breastfeeding Support Demonstration]

To qualify for childbirth support and certified labor doulas, participants must be at least 20 weeks pregnant, plan to give birth outside a military treatment facility (MTF), and must see a TRICARE-authorized provider for the birth event.

The program covers up to six hours of visits by a certified labor doula. The hours can be split into 15-minute increments. An untimed visit during birth is also covered.

For lactation or breastfeeding support services, the beneficiary must be at least 27 weeks pregnant and qualify for TRICARE’s breastfeeding support benefit, which covers breastfeeding counseling by TRICARE-authorized independent board-certified lactation consultants and certified lactation counselors as part of an inpatient maternity stay, outpatient visit, or well-child care visit.

[RELATED: Pilot Program Offers PCS Child Care Benefit]

In addition to the six sessions provided by the support benefit, the CBSD now covers breastfeeding counseling in a group setting. The lactation services come at no additional cost if the provider is in network.

The CBSD doesn’t cover telehealth labor doula services or MTF services. Telehealth breastfeeding support is available.

text:
Editor’s Note: This article is part of MOAA’s 2026-27 TRICARE Guide, brought to you by MOAA Insurance Plans, administered by Association Member Benefits Advisors (AMBA). A version of the guide appeared in the November 2026 issue of Military Officer magazine.

At the end of each year, MOAA’s Government Relations team assesses the legislative and policy landscape and establishes advocacy priorities for the year ahead. Because meaningful legislative and policy changes often require sustained effort, many priorities carry over from year to year.

MOAA must also be prepared to respond when new issues emerge. During the 119th Congress, two developments involving the military health system (MHS) became priority issues for MOAA.

First, coverage for certain GLP-1 medications was unexpectedly eliminated for TRICARE For Life (TFL) beneficiaries. Second, MOAA received indications that significant changes to TRICARE could be under consideration.

On Aug. 31, 2025, the TRICARE Pharmacy Program unexpectedly ceased coverage for certain GLP-1 medications for TFL beneficiaries. The decision was unprecedented in that it excluded a single beneficiary category from coverage for certain prescription drugs.

[RELATED: New Medicare GLP-1 Program Excludes TRICARE For Life Beneficiaries]

Since the announcement, MOAA has held multiple meetings with Defense Health Agency (DHA) officials and Pentagon leaders, and the association continues to advocate for reversal of the policy. We are also working to identify a champion in Congress to lead efforts to restore GLP-1 coverage for TFL beneficiaries.

Meanwhile, a provision in the Senate Armed Services Committee’s markup of the FY 2027 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) for a study on the MHS indicates major changes to TRICARE are in contemplation. While there are no current proposals for TRICARE reform, MOAA is monitoring the issue and is preparing for a quick response as the situation develops.

Addressing Access-to-Care Problems

As the 119th Congress draws to a close, improving access to care has remained MOAA’s top military health care priority. Top senior enlisted leaders for the Air Force, Army, Marine Corps, Navy, and Space Force underscored the importance of this issue at a February congressional hearing, telling lawmakers that access to health care is the top complaint they hear from servicemembers.

[RELATED: Senators Question Whether Military Pharmacy Program Is the Best Deal for Beneficiaries]

With a mission to represent beneficiaries, MOAA has limited visibility into the root causes of MHS access-to-care challenges. Our advocacy therefore focuses on practical solutions that can help beneficiaries navigate the MHS, expanding flexibility for self-directed care outside of military treatment facilities (MTFs), and improving transparency and accountability on access-to-care problems.

MOAA made significant progress against these goals with the introduction of the bipartisan Military Care Access, Reporting, and Evaluation (Military CARE) Act. This bill would:

Address access-to-care gaps by creating a secure, standardized digital platform for TRICARE beneficiaries to submit and monitor care concerns.

Require real-time notifications to patient advocates.

Direct the DHA to analyze complaint trends quarterly.

Require annual reports to Congress detailing access challenges and corrective actions.

[RELATED: NDAA Provision Would Help Remove Health Care Barriers]

MOAA worked with the office of Rep. Steven Horsford (D-Nev.) to develop this legislation, which Reps. Jen Kiggans (R-Va.), Chrissy Houlahan (D-Pa.), and Don Bacon (R-Neb.) also led.

In addition, MOAA members took the Military CARE Act to Capitol Hill during our spring Advocacy in Action event, raising awareness about access-to-care problems and urging lawmakers to support the legislation. As of this writing, there is a path forward for the Military CARE Act through the FY 2027 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA). The legislation is included in the Senate Armed Services Committee’s markup, and MOAA is working to ensure the language is included in the final version of the annual defense authorization bill.

Additional Priorities

description:

text:
Two Marines are suing the Defense Department over a breach of the Defense Manpower Data Center’s information system that exposed the personal information belonging to more than 3 million people with ties to the U.S. military.

The lawsuit, filed Tuesday in federal court in the District of Columbia, alleges that the department violated the Privacy Act of 1974 by failing to safeguard sensitive personal information and implement adequate cybersecurity controls despite internal warnings.

In July, the DMDC discovered a vulnerability in its file sharing system that allowed a “small number of unauthorized users” to access a massive swath of sensitive data, including full names, dates of birth, Social Security numbers, contact information, military jobs and other records, for nearly nine months. The department didn’t notify affected individuals of the breach until late September.

The plaintiffs, Active-duty Marine Tristyn Edwards and Marine veteran Morgan Stampfli, said the Pentagon exhibited “flagrant disregard for the privacy interests of service members and other military-adjacent individuals” and “refused to take steps to implement appropriate administrative, technical and physical safeguards to insure the security and confidentiality of records as required by the Privacy Act.”

The complaint cites inspector general reports dating back to 2021 that warned the department about problems with its cybersecurity practices but continued to “intentionally and willfully disregard its cybersecurity responsibilities.”

“Had DoD properly implemented standard cybersecurity controls — such as regular review of accounts, scanning for vulnerabilities, field encryption or tokenization of sensitive [personal information] and routine monitoring of system logs for suspicious activity — the data breach could have been avoided,” the plaintiffs argue.

“The DoD’s history of persistent, knowing non-compliance with [Federal Information Security Management Act’s] legal requirements ultimately resulted in the substantial harm, embarrassment, inconvenience or unfairness that [the Privacy Act] is designed to protect against,” they added.

The plaintiffs said they experienced multiple fraudulent charges on their financial accounts and “drastic” increases in spam calls and emails.

Edwards said the data breach will continue to harm him and other affected individuals for years as a result of the department’s “ineffective data security measures,” including identity theft, fraudulent charges and new lines of credit opened without their permission.

In addition, Edwards argues that identity theft could jeopardize his employment because he needs to maintain a security clearance for his work.

Stampfli said he experienced an unauthorized online purchase on his Navy Federal Credit Union debit card, and his email address was registered for a large number of newsletters and mailing lists.

When the Defense Department disclosed the incident in September, a Pentagon official told Federal News Network that there is “no indication that anyone’s personal information has been misused.”

The plaintiffs seek to represent more than three million impacted individuals and are seeking more than $5 million in damages.

The FBI suffered a major data breach around the same time the Defense Department disclosed its security breach.

title: Which patients receive evidence based psychotherapy? | Carmen McLean - LinkedIn
description:
I'm happy to share this new study on evidence-based psychotherapy for PTSD in the Military Health System.
Using data from 3,459 service members receiving behavioral health care at eight military treatment facilities, we used natural language processing to identify psychotherapy sessions involving prolonged exposure, cognitive processing therapy, or EMDR, and machine-learning to examine factors associated with treatment receipt.
We found a substantial drop-off between treatment initiation and treatment dosage: -51.3% initiated an evidence-based psychotherapy session -25.7% received at least three sessions within 90 days -7.5% received at least eight sessions within 14 weeks The strongest factors associated with evidence-based psychotherapy receipt included the total number of psychotherapy sessions, spacing between sessions, military service branch, and comorbid mood disorder.
These findings highlight the critical role of care processes—including scheduling access, provider availability, patient engagement, and clinic capacity—in supporting sustained access to evidence-based PTSD treatment.
STRONG STAR Consortium, Consortium for Defense Psychology, NATIONAL CENTER FOR PTSD

My husband and I have used Express Scripts for quite a number of years and are thankful for this benefit. We have never had an issue until now, and can’t help wonder if it has to do with the Evernorth affiliation.

After years of maintaining a 120/80 average blood pressure reading on a calcium channel blocker, my BP began climbing in February. After a number of different blood tests, CT scans, MRI, and more tests with normal results, the cardiologist increased dosage which caused edema and did not lower BP so a diuretic was added which also caused new side effects and did not lower BP. So my doctor reviewed my history of previous issues with BP meds as well as my pharmacogenomic and Hypertension DNA results and identified a medication that according to DNA tests showed I had normal enzyme activity needed to metabolize this new med as well as a functional vascular gene for the renin inhibitor to decrease function, potentially leading to a reduction in BP.

Before placing the order for the new drug I called Express Scripts to see if the med was covered and available. I was told yes. My doctor placed the order with a local pharmacy, who informed me that they cannot fill the order as they do not have nor can they get that medication. So, my doctor ordered the med directly from Express Scripts (ES) for a dose of 1/2 tab for 30 days. ES responded by providing a list of alternative drugs, some of which I had previously tried resulting in side effects and/or no reduction in BP due to my genetic variants. My doctor responded quickly to ES with information as to why this med was being ordered. Then a day or 2 later ES denied the order because they did not think 1/2 tab would provide a therapeutic dose. Again, due to my genetic variants I had to decrease dosage of other BP meds and Plavix in the past due to harmful side effects from taking the recommended dosage. So, my doctor responded quickly and ordered the recommended 1 tab per day for 90 days. It took another day or 2 to approve that order, another day or 2 to process it, another day or 2 before they shipped it, and now another 3-4 days before it arrives.

Meanwhile, during this nearly 3 weeks of ES dinking around with the medication order my BP has climbed to over 200/100 putting me at risk of a stroke. This never happened before with Express Scripts when medications or dosage was changed for my BP meds. This new medication isn’t new, it was FDA approved in 2007. Why is a prescription for a BP med being micromanaged and who is making these decisions? Is it a doctor, a pharmacist, a clerical worker, a pharmaceutical rep? Are they knowledgeable about the enzyme activity of my cytochrome P450 genes to insure I can metabolize the med, or do they know the function of my cardio, vascular, and renal genes to insure the med can block, inhibit, or reduce the function of the gene in order to reduce my BP when in reality 9 of those 17 genes actually have no function, and do they know the health issues and permanent damage I’ve had from BP meds in the past? They do not, but my doctor knows all of that as do I.

You would have thought my doctor had ordered a high dose of a controlled substance not a low dose of a BP meds. By the way, other than a BP med or two, and a year on Plavix (which had to be reduced to 1/2 of a 75mg tab every other day because side effects and a P2Y12 test showed I was at risk of a spontaneous bleed), and an antibiotic as needed in the past for a gum infection, I do not take any other pharmaceuticals and rarely an OTC such as cough syrup.

title: TRICARE Young Adult premiums to hit nearly $900 a month in 2027
description:
Military dependents in their early 20s will face health insurance premiums as high as $900 per month starting Jan. 1.
The Defense Health Agency quietly rolled out next year’s premiums for TRICARE Young Adult plans in the insurance program’s latest operations manual.
TRICARE gives them two options: Young Adult Select, which offers a higher deductible (up to $198 in 2026) with more flexibility to choose providers, for $394 per month; or Young Adult Prime, which typically has no deductible but requires specialist referrals, for $893 each month.
In comparison, enrollment in either TRICARE Prime or TRICARE Select is free for active-duty families.
Prime premiums have spiked over the past decade, while Select premiums have risen more gradually.
text:
Military dependents in their early 20s will face health insurance premiums as high as $900 per month starting Jan. 1.

The Defense Health Agency quietly rolled out next year’s premiums for TRICARE Young Adult plans in the insurance program’s latest operations manual. Those plans are designed for military dependents between ages 21 and 26 — once they’re no longer eligible to stay on a sponsor’s plan but haven’t yet aged out of TRICARE.

TRICARE gives them two options: Young Adult Select, which offers a higher deductible (up to $198 in 2026) with more flexibility to choose providers, for $394 per month; or Young Adult Prime, which typically has no deductible but requires specialist referrals, for $893 each month. That’s an 8.5% increase for Select members and a 12.5% bump for Prime members over last year’s premiums.

The new rates mean enrollees will dole out about $4,700 for Select or more than $10,700 for Prime over the course of the year, not including the additional costs of the care they receive.

In comparison, enrollment in either TRICARE Prime or TRICARE Select is free for active-duty families. Employer‑sponsored plan premiums in 2025 averaged $9,325 per year for one person and $26,993 for a family, according to KFF.

Prime’s monthly price tag is “beyond the reach of most young adults and a financial burden on their families,” Eileen Huck, the director of government relations for the National Military Family Association, told Federal News Network Wednesday.

Prime premiums have spiked over the past decade, while Select premiums have risen more gradually. Select’s monthly installments haven’t quite doubled, growing from $228 in 2016 to $394 in 2027. Prime’s have nearly tripled from $306 to $893 in that same time.

“Unlike other plans, TRICARE Young Adult beneficiaries must absorb the full cost of the plan,” Huck said. “There’s no government subsidy, and so we’ve seen the cost of that plan increase significantly.”

It’s unclear what’s causing Young Adult Prime’s premiums to snowball. The Defense Health Agency did not immediately respond to emailed questions Wednesday, and Huck’s group said the agency hasn’t adequately answered queries on the data behind the cost increases.

“Families facing higher premiums deserve a clear explanation of what’s driving them,” NMFA wrote in a release Wednesday.

NMFA notes the price hike could force dependents to look at other insurance options, like a parent’s employer-sponsored plan, an Affordable Care Act-compliant plan through federal and state insurance marketplaces or Medicaid.

The group is pushing Congress to pass a law allowing military dependents to automatically stay on a sponsor’s TRICARE plan until age 26, to mirror the limit set for commercial plans under the Affordable Care Act. But growing the number of people who are eligible for a heavily subsidized TRICARE plan would also increase the price of running the federal program.

“There is bipartisan legislation in both the House and Senate to make that change,” Huck said, “but it comes with a cost, and we haven’t been able to find a way to overcome that.”

TRICARE’s open enrollment season, when members can pick a new plan for the upcoming year, runs from Nov. 9 to Dec. 8. Coverage begins Jan. 1.

OCTOBER 21, 2026 – TRICARE Open Season begins Monday, Nov. 9. If you’re eligible for TRICARE, this is your chance to enroll in a health plan or change plans for coverage that starts Jan. 1, 2027. You can make eligible changes through Tuesday, Dec. 8. Keep reading for answers to common questions about TRICARE Open Season.

Does TRICARE Open Season apply to me?

TRICARE Open Season applies to you if you have or are eligible for one of these plans:

TRICARE Prime

Uniformed Services Family Health Plan

TRICARE Prime Demo

TRICARE Prime Remote

TRICARE Prime Overseas

TRICARE Prime Remote Overseas

TRICARE Select

TRICARE Select Overseas

How do I know if open season doesn’t apply to me?

Open season doesn’t apply to you if:

You’re an active duty service member.

You’re 65 or older and have TRICARE For Life coverage. This coverage starts automatically once you have Medicare Part A and Part B.

You have a premium-based plan, such as TRICARE Reserve Select, TRICARE Retired Reserve, or TRICARE Young Adult. You can purchase these plans at any time during the year.

What are my options during open season?

If TRICARE Open Season applies to you, you have three options:

Stay in your current plan. You don’t need to take any action to keep your coverage.

Enroll in a plan. If you don’t have a TRICARE health plan now, you can enroll during open season if you qualify.

Change your plan. Before you switch, check that your family’s information is current in the Defense Enrollment Eligibility Reporting System. Contact your service’s personnel office if you have questions about eligibility.

How do I make changes to my plan during open season?

There are three ways to enroll in a TRICARE health plan or change your plan.

Online:Go to milConnect.

By phone:

East Region: Call Humana Military at 800-444-5445.

West Region: Call TriWest Healthcare Alliance at 888-874-9378.

USFHP: VisitUniformed Services Family Health Plan for contact information.

TRICARE Prime Demo(Atlanta, Georgia and Tampa, Florida areas only): VisitTRICARE Prime Demo for more information and to see if it’s available where you live.

By mail or fax:Send an enrollment form to your TRICARE contractor.

How do TRICARE Prime and TRICARE Select compare?

TRICARE Prime and TRICARE Select are the two main TRICARE health plan options, and each works differently. Here are the key differences to consider before you choose:

Primary care manager. TRICARE Prime requires you to use a PCM who coordinates your care. TRICARE Select lets you see any TRICARE-authorized provider without choosing a PCM, as described in the TRICARE Choices in the United States Handbook.

Referrals. TRICARE Prime requires referrals for most specialty care. TRICARE Select doesn’t require referrals for most specialty care.

Availability. TRICARE Prime is available only in Prime Service Areas, generally near military hospitals and clinics. TRICARE Select is available everywhere.

Costs. TRICARE Prime has fixed copayments and no annual deductible. TRICARE Select has an annual deductible and charges cost-shares based on a percentage of the bill.Visit Health Plan Costs to compare costs side by side.

2027 costs will be available in November 2026. TRICARE Open Season is your chance to choose the health plan that fits your family’s needs. Don’t wait! Start reviewing your options today.

Halt to MTF Restructuring

What: The House NDAA would halt plans to close or cut services at more than 40 MTFs and require updated reporting criteria for any proposed MTF downsizing or closure.

What Else: The Senate NDAA does not include specific language to undo these changes, but a separate provision would require “comprehensive review” for any Pentagon moves to “downsize, realign, or otherwise reduce the scope of services” at MTFs. The process mandates a “consultative discussion” with the House and Senate Armed Services Committees at least a year prior to any such changes.

MOAA’s Role: Maintaining access to care is a key part of a world class health care benefit. We will continue to support proposals like these in the NDAA and other venues to ensure any cuts or access restrictions are supported by a rigorous analysis of civilian care availability and include mitigation efforts that will allow beneficiaries to find reliable care alternatives.

[RELATED: House and Senate NDAA Versions Differ on Your 2027 Raise]

A Strong Pharmacy Benefit

What: Both House and Senate NDAA versions require an audit of the TRICARE pharmacy program, to include “the adequacy of the retail pharmacy network.” The audit must pay special attention to rural and underserved areas.

What Else: The provisions require the audit to assess “meaningful geographic access standards beyond drive-time calculations” as part of the evaluation, as well as “continuity of care and beneficiary preference” standards.

MOAA’s Role: We’ve heard from many of our members about pharmacy access problems that speak to the need for this independent evaluation of the TRICARE retail pharmacy network. MOAA already successfully advocated for an initial report on beneficiary impact of retail pharmacy network cuts that indicated an additional 98,000 beneficiaries no longer have a pharmacy within distance-based access standards, 55% more than before the network cuts made in 2022. We appreciate that this new report requirement responds to MOAA’s concerns about the retail network outlined in our statement for the July 15 Senate Armed Services Personnel Subcommittee hearing on the TRICARE Pharmacy program.

[RELATED: 4 Priorities for a Stronger TRICARE Pharmacy Program]

Breaking Access Barriers

What: The Senate NDAA version includes language requiring the Pentagon to develop a new system for beneficiaries to file complaints about access-to-care issues, ensure those complaints can be tracked and forwarded to proper patient advocates, and submit annual reports to Congress on the number and type of complaints submitted.

What Else: The House version includes two provisions that acknowledge the need for improved problem reporting systems. One provision requires a feasibility study of a digital access complaint system. The other directs the Pentagon to set forth the process and timeline for beneficiaries and providers to report TRICARE issues that have not been resolved through existing channels.

MOAA’s Role: The MOAA-backed, bipartisan Military CARE Act (H.R. 6796) forms the basis of the Senate provision. Whether it’s a problem securing an appointment, issues after a PCS move, or other barriers to access, a robust data-collection system will not only help the Pentagon address common complaints, it will provide legislators and military health system leadership with the information needed to keep the system accountable.

[RELATED: TRICARE Closes Coverage Gap After Push From MOAA, Other Advocacy Groups]

The House and Senate are working to resolve differences between their respective versions of the FY 2027 NDAA. Please visit MOAA’s legislative action center to support the Military CARE Act and other health care priorities to help ensure they are included in the final version of the bill.

title: TRICARE Closes Coverage Gap After Push From MOAA, Other Advocacy Groups
description:

TRICARE began covering Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) earlier this year, according to a press release from medical technology company Monteris Medical.
A similar success story came earlier in 2025, when DHA announced provisional coverage for a drug treating early stage Alzheimer’s disease.

text:
One of two emerging TRICARE coverage gaps highlighted by MOAA and fellow advocacy groups last year has been closed, the latest success in ongoing efforts to ensure the plan keeps pace with private-sector care.

TRICARE began covering Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) earlier this year, according to a press release from medical technology company Monteris Medical. The procedure allows surgeons to target brain lesions and other abnormal brain tissue with greater accuracy, including in areas of the brain where the abnormalities could cause drug-resistant epilepsy.

While Medicare and other private sector plans already covered the procedure, TRICARE as of 2025 still considered LITT to be an unproven technique. MOAA and fellow members of The Military Coalition – a group of dozens of organizations representing about 5.5 million members of the wider uniformed services community – highlighted this coverage gap in a 2025 letter to the Defense Health Agency (DHA).

A similar success story came earlier in 2025, when DHA announced provisional coverage for a drug treating early stage Alzheimer’s disease. MOAA and The Military Coalition pushed for the closure of that coverage gap in 2024.

[RELATED: New Login Process Coming Soon for Military Treatment Facility Users]

More Work Remains

DHA has yet to address a coverage gap involving JAK inhibitors for patients with alopecia areata, an autoimmune disorder that leads to hair loss. Medicare and many private sector providers cover the medications (Litfulo and others).

Other TRICARE coverage gaps targeted by MOAA and fellow advocates include:

Chiropractic care and acupuncture for pain management.

Reproductive services, to include in vitro fertilization.

Coverage of young adult dependents (under age 26) in line with commercial plan requirements (and without the significant added costs faced by those using the TRICARE Young Adult plan).

[RELATED: NDAA Provision Would Help Remove Health Care Barriers]

MOAA also continues its work to reverse the 2025 decision to discontinue coverage of GLP-1 weight loss drugs for TRICARE For Life (TFL) beneficiaries (except those taking the drugs to treat Type 2 diabetes). As more GLP-1 options emerge under Medicare Part D and other health plans, it’s become clear DHA must address this issue to ensure those covered by TFL are not unfairly excluded.

Not only are some of these beneficiaries forced to choose between life-changing treatment and financial well-being, all current and future TFL users could see reductions in drug coverage should this move trigger a two-tier (TRICARE/TFL) pharmacy system.

text:
This article by Karen Jowers originally appeared on Military Times, the nation's largest independent newsroom dedicated to covering the military and veteran community.

To military parents who are frustrated because they can’t get access to their teenagers’ medical records, the U.S. Army Surgeon General has a message: “We share your concern,” and are working to address it.

Currently, parents don’t have access to a child’s medical records from the time they turn 13, “based on current departmental policy,” Lt. Gen. Mary K. Izaguirre said Tuesday at the annual meeting of the Association of the United States Army.

In addition, children don’t have ID cards to sign in to the Defense Enrollment Eligibility System (DEERS), she said. Children must be at least 18 to log in to the system.

[RELATED: Pilot Program Offers PCS Child Care Benefit]

The question of parents’ access came up during a family forum at AUSA. Izaguirre said the issue is one of her husband’s favorite topics, and “I share his passion for it,” she said.

For now, parents must go to the patient administration offices at their military treatment facilities and have their teenage children sign consent forms to give parents permission for access to their medical records.

“That’s a barrier,” Izaguirre said, adding that “we’ve been working with the [Defense Health Agency], and the [Department of Health and Human Services]” to address the hurdle.

The issue stems from privacy laws and has come up in various settings with military families.

[RELATED: Pentagon Schools Struggle to Identify, Support Children With Learning Disabilities]

Researchers with the organization Feedback were “surprised at how often this came up, not just one parent at one base,” said Erin Domagola, the research director at the organization. Feedback analyzed comments received in the Federal Register, following a Defense Department solicitation in March for comments and suggestions from military families on how DoD could improve their quality of life.

Feedback uses applied anthropology, behavioral science and digital ethnography to understand what people experience and why.

The company independently analyzed Federal Register military family comments from 2024 to 2026 about quality of life. While there were a relatively small number of comments overall —117 in 2026 — it does provide a window into some of the concerns and suggestions, the researchers said.

title: TRICARE Young Adult Premiums Are Rising Again: What Military Families Should Know
description:
Military families with young adult dependents who are enrolled in, or planning to enroll in, TRICARE Young Adult (TYA) should prepare for another premium increase in 2027, and this one is a doozy.
Unlike regular TRICARE coverage for eligible dependent children, TYA requires families or young adults to pay monthly premiums to maintain coverage.
While both options have increased, TYA Prime premiums have grown substantially faster, widening the disparity between the two plans.
Military Families Deserve Answers TRICARE Young Adult was created to extend health coverage to eligible young adults during a period when maintaining insurance can be challenging.
But with Prime premiums exceeding $10,000 annually in 2027, affordability is becoming an increasingly important consideration for military families.
text:
Military families with young adult dependents who are enrolled in, or planning to enroll in, TRICARE Young Adult (TYA) should prepare for another premium increase in 2027, and this one is a doozy. It’s the latest in a series of increases that have made coverage increasingly expensive, particularly for families choosing TYA Prime.

According to the Defense Health Agency’s (DHA) TRICARE Operations Manual, monthly premiums for 2027 will increase to $893 for TYA Prime and $394 for TYA Select. That’s an increase of $99 per month for Prime and $31 per month for Select compared to 2026.

For families paying for TYA Prime, the new rate means an annual premium cost of $10,716, an increase of $1,188 over 2026.

NMFA identified the new rates in the TRICARE Operations Manual incidentally, as they’ve not been made available through beneficiary-facing communications just yet. Under the program’s notification requirements, the government provides updated premium rates to TRICARE contractors, Humana Military and TriWest, at least 60 calendar days before they take effect. Contractors must then notify enrollees in writing of premium changes at least 30 calendar days before the effective date.

NMFA is concerned about what these rising costs mean for military families, particularly those relying on TYA to maintain health coverage for their adult children.

But beyond the sticker shock, there are important questions about how premiums are calculated, what’s driving the rising costs, and why TYA Prime has become significantly more expensive than TYA Select.

What Is TRICARE Young Adult?

TRICARE Young Adult is a premium-based healthcare program that allows eligible adult children of TRICARE sponsors to purchase coverage after they lose regular TRICARE eligibility, generally at age 21, or age 23 if enrolled in college and meeting eligibility requirements.

TYA provides coverage until age 26, as long as the young adult remains eligible. To qualify, young adult dependents must generally be unmarried, not eligible for employer-sponsored health coverage based on their own employment and meet other program requirements.

Depending on eligibility and location, beneficiaries can choose between two options:

TYA Prime generally requires enrollment with an assigned primary care manager and follows Prime’s referral and network rules.

TYA Select offers greater flexibility in choosing TRICARE-authorized providers, although out-of-pocket costs and other coverage requirements differ.

Unlike regular TRICARE coverage for eligible dependent children, TYA requires families or young adults to pay monthly premiums to maintain coverage.

How Much Have Premiums Increased?

When TYA launched in 2011, monthly premiums were $213 for Prime and $186 for Standard, the predecessor to Select. At the time, the difference between the two options was just $27 per month.

But beginning January 1, 2027, that gap will reach $499 per month, or nearly $6,000 annually.

While both options have increased, TYA Prime premiums have grown substantially faster, widening the disparity between the two plans.

To put that into perspective, TYA Prime cost $2,556 annually in 2011. In 2027, that same coverage will cost $10,716 annually. That’s an increase of $8,160, or approximately 319% since the program launched.

And the increases have accelerated significantly in recent years.

In 2021, TYA Prime premiums were $459 per month. Come January 1, 2027, they’ll reach $893. That means TYA Prime premiums will have increased nearly 95% in just six years.

TYA Select premiums have also increased, but at a considerably slower pace. From $186 per month in 2011 to $394 in 2027, Select premiums have increased about 112%.

Of course, TYA Select beneficiaries may face higher out-of-pocket costs when accessing care. But the difference in cost-sharing alone doesn’t explain why Prime premiums have increased so much more dramatically.

For military families comparing coverage options, the growing difference raises important questions: Why are TYA Prime premiums rising so significantly, and what’s driving the growing cost difference between the two coverage options?

How Are TYA Premiums Determined?

Unlike many other TRICARE coverage options, TYA is required by federal law to operate on a full-cost premium basis. Under Title 10, United States Code, Section 1110b, premiums must be established annually that are equal to the cost of providing coverage through the TYA program.

In response to NMFA’s inquiry about the 2027 increases, DHA confirmed the 2027 rates found in the TRICARE Operations Manual and explained that separate premiums are established for TYA Prime and Select under federal regulations. DHA also stated that premiums are adjusted annually based on TYA enrollee healthcare utilization during preceding years.

Essentially, premiums are tied to the cost of providing coverage to the enrolled population within each plan, rather than an individual beneficiary’s healthcare needs or expenses. Those costs are what help determine the monthly premium charged to beneficiaries.

However, DHA’s explanation did leave some important questions unanswered.

For example, what specific changes in healthcare utilization or costs have contributed to the increases? How much of the growth is attributable to medical expenses, enrollment patterns, or other factors? And why have those costs increased so much more dramatically for TYA Prime than TYA Select?

These are important distinctions for families trying to understand why their premiums continue to rise exponentially each year.

NMFA Is Asking for More Information

NMFA initially reached out to DHA to confirm the 2027 premium rates and to request additional information on how premiums are calculated, particularly the factors contributing to the substantial increases in TYA Prime.

DHA confirmed that the published rates are correct and explained the federal requirements governing premium calculations.

While their initial response clarifies DHA’s “legal obligation,” it doesn’t fully explain the underlying factors driving the increases.

NMFA has requested additional information, including:

Historical healthcare utilization data.

Details about the methodology used to calculate premiums.

An explanation of the widening cost difference between TYA Prime and Select.

As of the publication of this article, NMFA has not yet received a response addressing those additional questions.

We recognize that DHA is required to follow federal law when establishing TYA premiums. Our questions are intended to help military families understand the calculations behind those costs and the factors contributing to the increases.

Families facing higher premiums deserve a clear explanation of what’s driving them.

NMFA will continue seeking information from DHA and share additional findings as they become available.

What Should Military Families Consider Before 2027?

For families currently enrolled in TYA, or considering enrollment, the upcoming premium changes may warrant a closer look at their healthcare coverage options.

TYA Prime and Select offer different approaches to accessing care, but the substantial difference in monthly premiums makes Select the more affordable option for most beneficiaries, even when accounting for additional out-of-pocket healthcare costs. However, families should still be sure to compare coverage options based on their young adult’s healthcare needs, preferred providers, expected out-of-pocket expenses, and eligibility for other coverage options before making changes.

Young adults may also want to compare TYA with a parent’s employer-sponsored insurance, Marketplace plans, or other coverage for which they may qualify.

While these alternatives may carry similar monthly premiums, employer contributions or income-based Marketplace subsidies can sometimes reduce what beneficiaries pay out of pocket. Eligibility for those savings varies, so comparing total costs is important.

Before canceling or switching plans, families should also understand enrollment requirements and coverage effective dates to avoid unintended gaps in coverage.

Why NMFA Continues to Push for Coverage Parity

The rising cost of TYA also underscores a longstanding concern for NMFA: military-connected young adults don’t have the same access to parental health coverage as many of their civilian counterparts.

Under the Affordable Care Act, young adults can generally remain on a parent’s health insurance plan until age 26 without purchasing a separate, full-cost coverage plan.

Military families, however, typically lose regular TRICARE dependent coverage when their children turn 21, or 23 if they qualify as full-time students. Unlike their civilian counterparts, young adult dependents have to purchase TYA to remain tied to their parent’s health coverage.

That’s why NMFA continues to support legislation such as the Health Care Fairness for Military Families Act, which would extend regular TRICARE dependent eligibility to age 26.

Military-connected young adults shouldn’t face an additional financial burden simply because their parent served. NMFA believes they should have access to the same age-based dependent coverage protections available to civilian families.

Military Families Deserve Answers

TRICARE Young Adult was created to extend health coverage to eligible young adults during a period when maintaining insurance can be challenging. But with Prime premiums exceeding $10,000 annually in 2027, affordability is becoming an increasingly important consideration for military families.

NMFA understands that federal law determines how TYA premiums must be established. Still, understanding the legal requirement is only part of the picture. Families also need to understand why the cost of providing that coverage has increased so significantly and what the numbers mean for their healthcare decisions.

NMFA will continue to ask those questions and advocate for policies that ensure military families have access to affordable, quality healthcare. We also invite you to tell us your story or send your lawmakers a letter through our Military Family Action Center.
